name: Amaziah (Father of Josha, mentioned in the genealogy of Simeon (1 Chron. 4:34))
title: Simeonite clan member, father of Josha
summary: Amaziah belongs to the genealogy of the tribe of Simeon as presented in 1 Chronicles 4, where he is listed as the father of Josha among the named leaders of the tribe. The broader context of the chapter shows how Simeonite family heads sought new grazing lands and expanded their settlements, even though the tribe was geographically incorporated within Judah's territory. The fact that Simeon's lineages were recorded in such detail suggests that the tribe preserved its identity and clan organization at a time when several of the smaller tribes were losing their distinctiveness. Amaziah thus represents a link in a chain of family leaders who carried forward Simeon's tribal affiliation through the generations.

keyEvents.title: Expansion of Simeonite settlements
keyEvents.description: The clans listed in the genealogy of Simeon sought new grazing areas and expanded their settlements, including toward Gedor. Amaziah's connection to this expansion is indirect, through his position among the named clan leaders in the register.

versions.summary: Amaziah is mentioned in 1 Chronicles 4:34 as the father of Josha, in a genealogy of leaders from the tribe of Simeon. He belonged to a group of heads who expanded their settlements and grazing lands. Although little is known about him personally, his family was part of the history of Simeon's tribal leadership during the time of the divided kingdom.

versions.reason: [minor] The title 'Simeonite clan leader' is somewhat imprecise. The text mentions Amaziah as the father of Josha, but it is not entirely clear that Amaziah himself was a clan leader. He may have been one indirectly through his connection to the list, but the text primarily refers to him as the father of Josha.; [minor] The role 'leader' is possible but uncertain. Amaziah is mentioned primarily as the father of Josha in the genealogy. It is Josha and others who are explicitly called 'princes' or 'heads'. A role such as 'ancestor' or 'clan member' might have been more precise, possibly supplemented with 'father'.; [minor] There are five keyEvents for a person mentioned only in one verse (1 Chr 4:34). The last three events (expansion of settlements, Gedor, the hill country of Seir) concern the tribe of Simeon generally and do not specifically link Amaziah to these events. It may be misleading to attribute them directly to him.; [minor] The phrasing 'the history of the leader of the tribe of Simeon' is grammatically unclear. It should read something like 'the history of the tribe of Simeon' or 'the story of the leaders of the tribes of Simeon'.; [minor] Footnotes are missing. A linguistic note on the name Amaziah (Hebrew: אֲמַצְיָה, 'Yahweh is strong') and a historical note on the location and role of the tribe of Simeon in southern Judah would have been useful.

versions.summary: In the genealogy of the tribe of Simeon in 1 Chronicles 4, Amaziah is mentioned as the father of Josha, one of the named leaders within the clan structures of the tribe. The context of the chapter describes how Simeonite family heads expanded their settlements and sought new grazing areas, testifying to the tribe's continued activity and organization despite being geographically incorporated into Judah's territory. Amaziah appears as a link in a lineage of leaders who maintained Simeon's tribal identity and clan structure during a period when many of the smaller tribes lost their distinct identity.

footnotes.text: The name Amaziah (Hebrew: אֲמַצְיָה, Amatsyah) is formed from the root verb אמץ ('amats, 'to be strong') and the theophoric suffix -yah, which points to Yahweh. The meaning is 'Yahweh is strong' or 'Yahweh has given strength.' This type of name is very common in Israelite naming tradition and appears among several biblical figures, including the king of Judah with the same name.

The tribe of Simeon originally received its territory within the borders of Judah (Josh 19:1–9), which led to the tribe being largely assimilated into Judah over time. Nevertheless, the genealogies in 1 Chron 4:24–43 show that the tribe of Simeon maintained a distinct identity with its own clan structures and leaders, especially during the period of the divided kingdom.

The expansion of the Simeonites' settlements to Gedor and the Seir mountains (1 Chron 4:39–43) is placed in the reign of King Hezekiah and testifies to migration movements among the southern tribes. Some scholars have suggested that 'Gedor' may be a scribal error for 'Gerar,' which would fit better with the geographical area near the Negev.

The genealogies in 1 Chron 4:24–43 serve not only a genealogical function but also legitimize claims to land. The listing of family heads along with their associated territories reflects an administrative practice known from the Israelite monarchy, where the tribes' rights to the land were documented and preserved for future generations.

The genealogies in Chronicles were likely collected and edited during the post-exilic period but are based on earlier sources. For the tribe of Simeon, these sources may date back to the time of the monarchy, when the tribe's administrative structure was still intact. The records served as an important tool for restoring national identity after the return from exile.
